entities.summary:
Ibi, an influential ancient Egyptian noble of the early Saite Period, served as the chief steward to Nitocris I, the God's Wife of Amun, during the pivotal reign of Pharaoh Psamtik I (664–610 BCE) of the Twenty-sixth Dynasty. His career unfolded amidst Egypt's resurgence from Assyrian domination, a period marked by a deliberate revival of traditional Egyptian culture and a consolidation of power under the Saite pharaohs. As the primary administrator for one of the most powerful religious and political figures in Upper Egypt, Ibi played a crucial role in managing vast estates, overseeing temple affairs, and maintaining the economic and ideological stability of Thebes, a vital religious center that had long resisted direct Northern control. His tomb, TT36, located in the el-Assasif necropolis on the West Bank of Luxor, provides invaluable insights into the administrative structures, religious beliefs, and artistic conventions of this transformative era.

Ibi's responsibilities as Chief Steward (imy-r pr wr) for Nitocris I were extensive, encompassing the daily management of her vast household, agricultural lands, and numerous temple endowments. Nitocris I, adopted by Shepenwepet II and Amenirdis II, represented the peaceful reunification of Egypt after the Assyrian withdrawal, her authority effectively extending Saite control over the traditionally independent Theban region. Ibi would have been instrumental in ensuring the efficient operation of this complex economic engine, which sustained the Amun priesthood and the court of the God's Wife. His administrative acumen would have been critical in overseeing the collection of revenues, the distribution of resources, and the maintenance of religious rituals, thereby reinforcing the legitimacy of both Nitocris I and the Saite pharaohs.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Ibi's career as a chief steward highlights the sophisticated administrative structures crucial to the Saite Dynasty's resurgence and the enduring power of the God's Wife of Amun. His well-preserved tomb, TT36, serves as a vital archaeological record, offering detailed insights into Saite Period governance, religious beliefs, and artistic practices.
